newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's GIA says states offered arms, cash - paper.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's GIA says states offered arms, cash - paper.

text.p: Algeria's radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA), locked in a five-year-old conflict with the Algerian government, said foreign governments offered to supply it with money and weapons, an Arab paper said on Sunday.

GIA chief Antar al Zouabri was quoted by the London-based Arabic language Al-Hayat newspaper as saying the GIA had broken its links with radical fundamentalist groups in Egypt and Libya because of ideological divergencies. He termed Libyan militants as being only "fundamentalists on paper".

"You have to know that the Armed Islamic Group has been offered material support, and not only moral support, from some regimes, which offered to supply it with weapons, ammunition, equipment and money," said al Zouabri quoted by Al-Hayat.
He did not identify these governments but said his group had rebuffed the offers.

The GIA, a ruthless Moslem fundamentalist organisation fighting to establish a purist fundamentalist state in the North African country, is blamed for killing civilians, including female activists, writers, journalists and religious workers.

It is also blamed for taking Algerian civil strife into French streets where eight people were killed and around 170 injured by bombs between July and October last year in Paris and the central city of Lyon.

The GIA's al Zouabri, dismissing the tide of outrage in Algeria following the killing of non-combatant civilians, said "there are many religious proofs which make legitimate (our) bombing operations even when there are civilian victims."
He made clear there had been cooperation between Egypt's Jihad (Holy War) and Libya's Combatant Armed Group and the GIA but it ended because of ideological in-fighting.
"It became clear after discussions with the Combatant Group that they are only fundamentalists on paper and all just talk... They are much close to the Moslem Brotherhood path," he said.
Moslem Brotherhood followers are seen as moderate activists seeking change through elections.

The statement carried by al Hayat was believed to be the first reported remarks ascribed to al Zouabri since he replaced Djamel Zitouni, who was killed last July near Larba, 25 km (15 miles) south of Algiers.
More than 50,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
